item.title: Rednecks are Comrades Too
item.description:
Originally published in News Not Bombs Vol 6 By Canton Food Not Bombs

What qualities come to mind when you think of a “redneck”? Is it someone who is uneducated, intolerant, and politically far-right? You may be surprised that the term “redneck” was actually used to describe people with strong lefist principles In 1921, the largest labor uprising in American history took place in West Virginia, known as the Battle of Blair Mountain.Around 10,000 coal miners battled 3,000 lawmen who were preventing them from unionizing. the union members wore a red bandana around their necks to symbolize their solidarity—thus, the term “redneck” was born out of working-class solidarity. Urban lefists must not dismiss the rural working class because of stereotypes but rather accept them as comrades and build solidarity with them.

item.title: Rediscovering Jesus
item.description: In the last few months I found myself returning to church officially after years of testing the waters. I experienced a wide section of the Christian denominational spectrum in my childhood that included Mennonite, Baptist, Charismatic Pentecostal, and others. For the most part my experience with religion was interwoven with familial conflict that spiraled into some fairly traumatic moments that left me with quite a bit of anxiety surrounding religious environments. I stepped away from religion and considered myself an atheist for some time.

item.title: The Dawn of Everything
item.description:
After more than a year of dipping in and out of this book, I finally got around to finishing Graeber and Wengrow's The Dawn of Everything, thanks to all the doctor's appointments and other opportunities for waiting around that come with being a foster parent. Not to mention throwing my smartphone into a lake (metaphorically).



I mostly read this for fun rather than in an academic sense and avoided the 150+ pages of footnotes. My main takeaway is simply that it was fun to learn about all sorts of different societies and their methods of organizing themselves—which is aided by the fact that part of the book's thesis is that prehistoric societies were much more diverse than the traditional story of "societies were simple, egalitarian hunter-gatherers until government was invented."

item.title: Worker's Councils
item.description: I started Workers Councils by Anton Pannekoek with my local IWW bookclub, but in my typical fashion, I fell behind after the first couple meetings. Exacerbated by the fact that my dog ripped the book half to shreds, I put it down for a while (the book not my dog). Last week I picked it back up and finally finished it. Most of the book was legible, luckily, save for a few pages in the back.

item.title: My Every-Day Carry
item.description:
Pictured above is what can most often be found in my pockets at any given time.


From top left to bottom right

Field Notes

This is my favorite item in my EDC and has been a game changer after replacing my smartphone. I use a pocket notebook for my to-do list, grocery list, random ideas, stuff to google later, and doodles. Anything important gets noted in Obsidian the next time I am at my desk. This helps me be more mindful and focused compared to using my phone for notes.

I also love the Field Notes brand and I am planning to buy all their national parks editions. But eventually I might get into making my own pocket notebooks.
